3. The case of the pre-emptor, is that, the pre-emptor himself is a co-sharer in 8(eight) annas share in SA khatian 305 appertaining to Borovila Mouja. His father was owner in possession in SA plots 1203, 1204, 1205, 1272, 1365 of Purbasreekol Mouja and in SA plots 3603, 4072, 4077, 8177 of Sreekol Mouja and in SA plots 81, 83, 120, 323, 405 of Borovila Mouja. He died leaving behind 2(two) sons named Safiuddin Mridha and Golam Sarwar. Thus the pre-emptor is a recorded tenant in plot 119 of SA khatian 305 and heir of other plots. The son and daughters of Golam Sarwar sold the case land in favour of opposite party 1 by the impugned documents dated 14-12-2010 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor came to learn about the sale from the husband of opposite party 1 on 17-12-2010 and got definite knowledge on 30-12-2010 after getting the certified copy. It is further stated that the pre-emptor and his brother purchased the land of SA plot 405 appertaining to SA khatian 280 by kabala dated 16-2-1972. Their father Bazlur Rahman sold the land of plot 323 of SA khatian 351 to Jamanat Ali through kabala dated 24-10-1962. Subsequently the land was purchased by pre-emptor and his brother from Jamanat Ali Molla by kabala dated 4-2-1971. Although Bazlur Rahman sold 20 decimals of land out of 41 decimals from plot 8171 of SA khatian 1180 but he had right, title, interest and possession in the remaining land. Their mother 365 also had title in plot 1262/21365 SA khatian 1647. Besides the pre-emptor is also an heir. in SA khatian 415. Thus the pre-emptor is the co-sharer by inheritance and purchase. The quantum of land owned by the pre-emptor does not exceed the ceiling. Hence the case for pre-emption was filed. 

 4. Opposite party 1 contested the case. Her case is that this pre-emption is not maintainable and the same suffers defect of party. The case is barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The pre-emptor and Golam Sarwar are 2(two) brothers. Golam Sarwar died leaving behind 1(one) son and 4(four) daughters who are opposite parties 2-6. These opposite parties 2-6 do not reside in the disputed mouja. Because of the necessity of sale they requested the pre-emptor to purchase the land. But pre-emptor expressed his inability to purchase the same and told opposite parties 2-6 to transfer the same elsewhere. Then opposite parties 2-6 assigned the pre-emptor to transfer the case land. Pre-emptor then asked opposite party 1 to purchase the land and negotiated and fixed the price and the transaction was done at his instance and, as such, this opposite party 1 purchased the land. Since pre-emptor gave consent to sell and also negotiated the sale his claim of pre-emption is barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in plot 1205 of SA khatian 415. Samed Mridha, Hamid Mridha, Amir Mridha, Samir Mridha are necessary parties being tenants in SA khatian 2172. Wazed Mridha is also a necessary party being tenant in SA khatian 1180. Pre-emptor is not a co-sharer because he transferred his interest to some other persons. The pre-emptor knew about the transfer from before. This opposite party 1 has not purchased the case land behind his back. The husband of this opposite party 1 neither asked the pre-emptor to abandon his claim in the case land nor the pre-emptor acquired knowledge of such transfer from her husband. The case of the pre-emptor being false is liable to be dismissed. 

 9. Mr Taposh Kumar Dutta, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that from a plain reading of the application for pre-emption it is not understood how the pre-emptor became co-sharer by inheritance in the case land. He points out that it was the duty of the pre-emptor to draw a clear picture on point of his co-sharership but the application does not even introduce the BS and RS khatians corresponding to SA khatians covering the land of the disputed sale. He also submits that some of the SA khatians have not been filed to make out a definite case on co-sharership and the same is also apparent from the third schedule of the application. He further submits that the sale by exhibit-Uma(1) dated 4-6-1982 was miscalculated by the trial Court because the transferors were Bazlur Rahman and 2(two) sons of Wakil Uddin both of whom got 1/3 share each. He drives our attention on the case of Abdul Karim vs Nurjahan Begum and others, 38 DLR 361 and submits that the vendors being brother's children the pre-emptor is in loco parentis with them and principle of estoppel is applicable where a case of acquiescence is made out. He finally submits that the trial Court erred in law in allowing pre-emption in part upon wrongful consideration and the impugned judgment being perverse is liable to be set-aside.
